result.summary: Eteocles and Polynices quarrel over Thebes, and Polynices flees to Argos, where Adrastus gives him and Tydeus his daughters. Eriphyle is bribed with the necklace to force Amphiaraus into the war, and the seven leaders march on Thebes. After Nemea, Tiresias's prophecy and many deaths, the brothers kill each other and only Adrastus escapes.

scenes.title: Exile and marriages at Argos
scenes.summary: The brothers agree to alternate rule, but Polynices is banished and at Argos fights Tydeus. Adrastus marries his daughters to both and promises to restore them.
scenes.stakes: Polynices risks losing his kingdom and his place of refuge.

scenes.title: Eriphyle bribed with necklace
scenes.summary: Amphiaraus foresees doom and resists the war. Polynices bribes Eriphyle with the necklace and she forces him to go.
scenes.stakes: Amphiaraus faces certain death in a war he foresees as doomed.

scenes.title: The seven leaders
scenes.summary: Adrastus musters the army and the seven leaders are listed, with variants.

scenes.title: Nemea and the funeral games
scenes.summary: Hypsipyle leaves the infant Opheltes to show a spring and a serpent kills him. The army founds the Nemean games in his honor.
scenes.stakes: The infant Opheltes is killed; Hypsipyle is a slave answerable for her charge.

scenes.title: Tydeus's embassy and the gates
scenes.summary: Tydeus demands the kingdom for Polynices, defeats the Thebans and kills the ambush. The Argives take posts at the seven gates and Eteocles arrays his men.
scenes.stakes: Tydeus risks death in single combat and ambush; Thebes risks conquest.

scenes.title: Tiresias and his blindness
scenes.summary: Different stories explain Tiresias's blindness and prophecy: Athena's anger, or Hera's after he judged love's pleasures.
scenes.stakes: Tiresias loses his sight for seeing what he should not or for his judgment.

scenes.title: Battle and deaths at Thebes
scenes.summary: Menoeceus sacrifices himself, Capaneus is struck down, the brothers kill each other and the leaders die. Amphiaraus is swallowed by the earth and Adrastus escapes on Arion.
scenes.stakes: The leaders face death; Tydeus loses immortality; Thebes faces defeat.

alias_notes.explanation: The boy is renamed Archemorus, 'beginning of doom', after the omen of his death.
Some say the charioteer of Amphiaraus was named Elato.

notable_quotes.reason: Tiresias's verdict on the pleasure of love, a famous part of his legend.

analysis.text: The passage shows fated doom and brotherly strife: bribery, broken agreements and prophecy drive the Seven against Thebes to ruin.
Aetiological details, such as the Nemean games' origin and the seven gates, tie the myth to real cult and places.

legacy.text: The story inspired Aeschylus's Seven against Thebes and Euripides's Phoenician Women, and later Statius's Thebaid.

fun_facts.text: The Nemean games were one of the four Panhellenic festivals of ancient Greece.

language_notes.text: The necklace and robe are the gifts of Harmonia, the cursed heirloom of Thebes' royal house, explained in the footnote and earlier chapters.
The seer's oracle said Adrastus's daughters would marry a boar and a lion; the shield emblems let him read the prophecy as fulfilled.
"Yoke his daughters in marriage" uses the image of harnessing animals to mean joining them to husbands.
"Forepart" means the front half of the animal, shown as the device on the shields.
"Made it up with him" means reconciled with him after a quarrel.
The bracketed number [572] is an editor's footnote marker, not part of the original; the same applies to the other bracketed numbers.
Nemea is a valley in the northeastern Peloponnese, near Argos; the name here refers to the district ruled by Lycurgus.
Refers to the Lemnian women's killing of the men of Lemnos; Hypsipyle had secretly saved her father Thoas, king of the island.
Archemorus means 'beginner of doom' or 'beginning of death', a name given because the child's death foretold the doom of the expedition.
Quoit is a heavy disc, like a discus, thrown in athletic contests.
The agreement was that Polynices and Eteocles would rule Thebes in alternate years; Eteocles refused to yield the throne after his year.
Divination means seeking knowledge of the future or the gods' will, here by examining omens.
Soothsayer: a prophet or seer who foretells events. Tiresias is the most famous seer of Theban legend.
Understanding birds refers to augury, divining the future from the cries and flight of birds.
Cadmeans: the Thebans, named for Cadmus, the legendary founder of Thebes.
"Did doughty deeds" means performed brave, valiant actions.
Amphiaraus, a seer, was famously swallowed by the earth alive and later honoured as a god with an oracle.
A Fury is one of the avenging goddesses. Demeter took this shape in the myth where Poseidon pursued her, so Arion's birth is unusual.

context_notes.text: Adrastus was king of Argos. Tydeus was an exile from Calydon, and Polynices an exile from Thebes, so both arrived as fugitives.
Amphiaraus was a famous seer of Argos and married to Eriphyle, Adrastus's sister, which explains why she could settle his disputes.
Ancient sources disagree on the Seven's membership; this variant replaces the two exiles Tydeus and Polynices with other Argive leaders.
Cithaeron is the mountain range between Boeotia and Attica, on the approach to Thebes.
Thebes was traditionally said to have seven gates, so each Argive champion is matched to one.
Hera is Zeus's wife and goddess of marriage; their quarrel over who enjoys love more is a famous story about Tiresias.
Ares is the god of war, so a human sacrifice to him was thought to secure victory in battle.
Eteocles and Polynices were sons of Oedipus, quarrelling over the throne of Thebes. Their mutual death fulfils their father's curse.

literary_notes.text: The seer knows the expedition will fail and still will be forced to join it, since his own oath hands the decision to his wife.
Amphiaraus's command to his sons to kill their mother anticipates the later matricide, the consequence of Eriphyle's bribe.
Amphiaraus, a seer, reads the infant's death as a sign of the coming disaster, and the new name Archemorus underlines it.
Tydeus' victories and the slaughter of fifty ambushers show him as fierce and formidable; sparing Maeon leaves a survivor.
Mortals punished for seeing or revealing what belongs to the gods is a recurring theme in Greek myth.
Capaneus, about to scale the walls, is struck down by Zeus in the act, a sharp reversal of his confidence.
The gruesome image of Tydeus eating the brains shows his savagery and explains why Athena turns away.
